A SLAYEHOLDINO REPUBLIC. From the London Saturday Review. Nothing can be more rational than the skepticism which leads men of experience to doubt the occurrence of any very great event which is very confidently predicted ; and if tire event be an American event, incredulity is increased by the knowledge that the American people have principles of barking which are entirely distinct from their princip es of biting. Still there are some symptoms which make it worth while to attend to the contingency of a separation between the Northern and Southern States of the Union. If there is one sign w hich clearly shows that an American is genuinely uneasy, it is the abatement of his commercial confidence, and we now learn that, as soon as it hi came more than the Presidency, American probable that Mr. Lincoln securities would he elected to declined seriou-ly in all parts of the United States. It does not seem to be thought lor one moment that any act of armed rebellion is meditated by the slaveholders, and they appear to be too divided in opinion for there to be much ehance of their concerting a plan of simultaneous resistance. But one or two Southern S ates, peopled by bigots of more than ordinarily to furious have announced that they mean take aeoutse temper, which is certainly alarming. They propose to instruct the Senators who lepresi iit theiu iu tbo Upper House of Cong, ess to r, sign l heir seats, and then they intend to abstain from filling the vacancies. The Senate, in which all States are equally represented, is the knot of the Federal

Union; but there do not s cm to be any means of compelling an unwilling Stan to contribute delegates to it, Dor is there any known Constitutional fictiou by which the itnpty places can be taken to be tilled. The withdrawal of a part ol the Senators would amount to a de facto' ' separation much more difficult to deal with, and perhaps more dangerous, than overt treason against the commonwealth. As soon as it becomes worth while to discuss the establishment of a separate federation of the Slaveowning States, the consider itions which sugge.-t themselves are such as to make us wonder at the lolly of the undertaking. The least drawback on it is its expensiveuexs. At prcseut, tho cost of the General Government is most South ; and, though unequally distributed iu between the Southern xectiou the North aud these expenses are much laiger than in tho N o thorn, tr im the gie.iter inaccessibility ot the country, tire amount contributed by the Slave States to the revenue which pays them is out of . proportion smaller than the amount raised all from the States of Free-Soil. This, however, is a trifling reason for valuing the Union, compared with others. Is it possible that the planters do not perceive that their connection with the Northern States has the effect, as it Were, of insuring their peculiar institution? Looked at impartially , it is much more like a contrivance for keeping up negro servitude than for weakening it. T he utmost outrage with which they are menaced by Mr. Lincoln and the Republicans

i< a Congressional measure prohibiting the introduction of Slavery into lite North- Western Territories of the Union. Even this disadvantage is not necessarily a consequence of the gress is still host lie to the Republicans, and the Southern planters, who ate unanimous themselves, and allied with a powerlul minority in every State of the North, have a reasonable prospect of even now thwarting their antagonists' policy. But if the Southern States once succeeded in constituting a separate Federation, it is surely clear that every question now pending between themselves and the North would become at. once an international question. Every point now at issue iu the domestic forum of Congress would come under the cognizance of the general society of nations. What sort of division of the unsettled territory now belonging to the United States would ever be agreed upon between the Northern and Southern Federations nobody cau pretend even to conceive ; and this is the very difficulty which seems to show that the severance could never be effected

without bloodshed, lit is plain, however, that every attempt of the Southern States to expand beyond tho territory absolutely secured to tliem would be resisted, not simply by their Northern neighbors, but by the whole strength of European civilization. T he more reckless spirits ot the South are pushing on their quarrel in the belief that, if they were once disembarrassed of the Union, they could rend province after province from Mexico, and fill each successive acquisition with their slaves. But Europe would have a word in the matter. It is simply the incorporation of the North with tin South which prevents European statesmen from treating the annexations of the United States as avowed extensions of the area of Slavery. They cannot now upbraid a Confederacy , of which more than half the menibeis have no slaves, with conquering and annexing merely in t lie interest of cotton and nigroes, but tin re w. uld be no scruple about taxing the Southern Federation with designs which it would be at no pains to conceal. Nor is there, we take it, the slightest doubt tbat the Free States would rather assist than impede the efforts of European diplomacy The Monroe doctrine would be destroyed by the very tact of separation, and a Northern Union, once divided from the South, would not be long in making the discouragement of Slavery the cardinal principle of its foreign policy. In short, the measure of the dangers of separation is the advantage now derived fiom disunion. Slavery

is sufficiently unpopular in the world for a mere slaveholding Commonwealth to run no small risk of becoming the victim of a general crusade. But the actual connection ol the Southern States with the North has the effect of masking their exclusive devotion to a hat d system The Constitution of tho United States, as experience has abundantly shown, can often be so managed as to promote the objects of the slave-owners, and whenever advantage is gained iu this Way, it is gained without incut ring danger, and almost without attracting attention. The extravagant notions of their own prowess entertained by the Ann ricatis of the Southern Statos has persuaded them that they would lose nothing in military strength and resource by casting off the bondage of the Constitution We can only say that England is the only country which has had a serious struggle with the United States, and English experience does not Lear out the Southern pretensions. During the Revolutionary War, the English troops scarcely commanded a foot of ground in the North which they did not actually occupy. But, later in the struggle, the Sottiii was all but subjugated; and had not the inconceivable strategy of the English Generals given a different turn to the issue, it seemed at one time probable that, eveu if New-England and the Middle States, obtained their independence, the mother would he left in possession of Georgia country and the Carolinas, just as site was of Canada and Nova- Scotia. Similarly, in the war of 1812, nobody

in England ever doubted tbat the Southern States were the vulnerable part of the Federation; nor has the result changed this opinion. The expedition to New-Oi leans, though wilfully given up to destruction by General Pakenham, was exceedingly well planned ; and had not the signing of peace in Europe interrupted hostilities, a second expedition on a larger scale aud under liott. r commanders, would as-nredly have ascended the Mississippi. It h not, indeed, to be supposed that anybody in England ever doubted, or doubts, the personal gallantry of the Southern whites. Even il the Southerner he somewhat ot a bully, we have no faith in the popular assumption that a bully is a poltroon. But we iii Europe have recently learned to distrust the strength of every system which is based on the depression of a subject population. There were brave men in Italy who we.e w. dded to the cause ol legitimacy þÿ such men, for example, as are still grouped around King Francis at Gaeta. But the lesson we have received is, that it is never safe to calculate on the abasedisdain the m gro as a rebel mote tlian the hardly ment of subjects. The Southerners can lo< a! Italian despots despised their p< onle as mutl neers. If the negio is considered half a, an " My people," wrote King Ferdinand, " bond tnal, the Italian was thought half a woman their Decks and obey." Yet a very slight assistance from without swept away the Italian tyrants; and for our part we do not envy tho Southern whites when once a negro Garibaldi is

'1'lit late Message of the President is as full of allusions to Divine Providence as the last dying speech and confession of a Newgate martyr. That he should, in the ultimate hour of his political and the penultimate hour of his physical existence, thus open diplomatic relations with Heaven, may strengthen orthodoxically the skeptical and assure the pious. Death-hed repentances are not especially recommended by Doctois of Divinity, and in all systems of theology are esteemed rather a risky reliance; hut we submit, with the modesty becoming laymen, that the President has been an extraordinary offender and should an lowed to exhibit his remorse in lie al- extraordinary way. We have been told so often, by so many smug Union-savers, that religion is one thing and politics are another þÿ that the one is oil and the second water that between the two þÿ affinity is morally impossible þÿ that any attempt at affiance must he followed by a louder explosion and a worse stench than was ever heard or smelt in a chemical lecture-room þÿ we have been told all this so frequently and so earnestly, that really we were beginning to question the compatibility of patriotism and piety. The President has kindly reassured us in his Message. No public document of modern times has about it a more agreeable aroma of religion. In the frankest and handsomest way, Mr. Buchanan is pleased in more places than one to acknowledge the existence of a

God, and not. merely of a remote, cold and unsympathizing Being, hut of a God who takes an interest in elections, watches over Congresses, by the aid of chaplains, and does not disdain even to inspire Message. the It composition been this must have of an Annual evidence of reviving grace which induced Dr. Spring, a good shepherd ot this city, to visit Washington, as we are told that he is now doing, that he may, by his advice, strengthen the virtuous and reclaim the wayward in these times of trial. We recommend the President to his attention ; tor that Functionary is evidently very near a point will at do which the choicest wheat whisky him no good whatever. This is clearly the lime to take him in hand þÿ now when he when he is telling us that " self-preser- is talking in such an edifying way þÿ now " valion is the first law" þÿ higher than any law of Congress, in fact, and simply the "higher law" þÿ " heart of Man by Ins Creator' now, "implanted þÿ in the when he is exclaiming : " My prayer "to God is that he would preserve the "Constitution and the Union" þÿ now, when he is admitting that "Sovereign " Stales are responsible to God" þÿ now when be is dilating with "Christian " charity" toward Mr. Abraham Lincoln þÿ now when lie is reminding us ot the " "solemn sanctions ot religion' now þÿ when, in behalf ot the nation, he is offei- 1 ing "grateful thanks to a merciful Providence." If Dr. Spring cannot bring him to a solemn sense ol his situation now, he would not believe though one

should rise from the dead. We remember once to have witnessed the admission into a certain Second Baptist Church ol' a penitent negro. I his brand, plucked and black from the burning, sat apart in a sort of gallery perch until the white sinners had been taken into fellowship; when the excellent pastor said, "John, come down !" And John did come down. The white neophytes

fr T. o H 0 (1 X avis- . bad been gently enough dealt with, but John, being black, caught it severely. "John," said the pastor, "you have been "a great sinner. You have been one of "the worst thieves, my brother, in this "neighborhood; you have been a filthy- " mouthed swearer, you have been a "beastly drunkard. (J know it massa.') "You now profess repentance; hut a "great many people think you will haek- " slide, and they have reason to think so. tl( Sartain , massa!) However, we will "give you a trial," «fcc. So John was admitted, and retired to his perch in a flood of tears. This will be a pretty story for Dr. Spring to relate to the President; and we hope that he will take care to dwell particularly upon the catastrophe of the chickens. It must be admitted that this access of religious fervor þÿ they are praying, by the way, mightily in South Carolina þÿ would iiave been quite as welcome several years ago as now. We wish we had heard something of this savory "Christian charily," when the Missouri borders were bringing back in Kansas a worse than the old Indian barbarity. We slio .Id like to have the President even now apply his just discovered "law of self-preservation implanted in " the heart of Man by his Creator" to the Fugitive Slave Law, the looped and windowed raggedness of which lie so i much laments. The religion of ejacu-

lation may be better than none. It the President will not pray at home, then let him pray at the corner ot the streets. It lie will not confess in bis closet, then let him profess hy proclamation. But we beg all his old" admirers þÿ the manhunters and man-owners who once voted |(,r him þÿ the defaulting Postmasters and the bullying catcbpoles who have eaten of his salt, and the pimple-nosed retainers who have broken beads in bis behalf : we beg the roughs of the Democratic party, men ol the fist, and men pen, when they are disposed to sneer ol the at one-sided fanatics ol the sin ol Havery, to remember that Mr. Buchanan has taken religion under his protection, and may set them a goodly example of to his cloth and ashes before lie has. sackown satisfaction, finished his purgation. While meteorologists are summing up their returns for the twelvemonth, the Registrargeneral has published his for tbe quarter, wherein is satisfactorily shewn that the muchccnsured season, with all its wind, rain, and stoims, lias been favourable to health, the deaths having been fewer by many thousands than in fotmer seasons, which were described as the very perfection of fine weather. In a former Month , wo called attention to Hr Stenhmtse's application of charcoal as a material for respirators, and as a disinfectant, an application which time and experience have abundantly verified. Many of our readers ktiow that the ventilation of sewers is a question which has long been discussed and never lo o ght to a satislactory conclusion ; they know also that the numerous grating- by which sewergases escape and rise into the streets are offensive and obnoxious to health, especially in narrow streets and crowded neighbourhoods. This is an acknowledged evil, hut the sewers must be ventilated, and the moie their contents are oxidised by admission ot air, the more harmless do they become. As the openings must not be closed, and ought indeed to be multiplied, it occurred to one of the sanitary officers in tbe city to adopt the principle of Dr Stenhouse's charcoal respirator, and having fitted a series of charcoal filters into the openings that lead from the sewers to the surface of tbe streets,

he finds tile solution of the important question, for the noxious gases are comph tely neutralised. Of course, special precautious have to be taken in the preparation of the shafts, and the fibers must he kept dry, or the charcoal will cease to act, hut ul the result there is no doubt ; the unpleasant smell is entirely destroyed. During the past two years, many parts of London, withiu the city, have been thus purified The openings need not necessarily be in roadways, they may be led up through the lamp pillars, or between party-walls, or into cltimueys A west-end engineer has tiied the same plan in purls of Westminster, and with the like success ; it is adopted in the dc w sewage-works at W est Ham ; it has been applied at Bowood, the scat of Lord Lattsdowne, and we hear talk of its introduction into Glasgow. Its general adoption can only be a question of time, for charcoal is the cheapest remedy yet thought of for the prevalent evil , it is applicable at outfalls as well as along the course of sewers, and if kept dry retains its efficacy tor many years. London, with i's hundieds of miles of sewers, would require 25 000 fillers. To be coutinued.

Professors Bunsen and Kircboff, of Heidelberg, to whom modern chemistry is largely indebted, have lately rmide a discovery which, in die va-t field it op, ns for further ie.-e«rcli, may be ranked us the most famous of the year. It is a method of chemical analysis by means of the spectrum. Most readers know that by spectrum is meant the rainbow beam reflected I torn a glass pi ism exposed to sunlight: it is producible also by the light ol a lamp, and chemists and opticians have at times experimented on the changes that appear when dif-

ferent substances are burned within the lumpflatne. A spectator in the European theatre may well be cnnti lit with the steady progress of the actiou, the poetical justice which is dealt forth, aud the stern fatality which points but to one Europe gradually coming catastrophe. Every influence which to exists is round work in in favour of the Italians. England uev. r did a greater service to a nation than when she demanded that the Italians should be left to themselves A people who cannot fight their own battles are worth nothing, aud the Sardinians, victorious at Ancona and Gaeta, must have far more confidence in themselves than if an Engl sli fleet had demolished the Papal or the B- urban batteries But the last success of Italian courage and perseverance is a inoral one. The German people are at length almost converted to the beliel that they have been throughout this affair the most illiberal and shortsighted politicians in Europe, with the exception of their own Princes aud Ministers. But a few months ago the vote of the Prussian Chamber would have been impossible, for eveu the Ltbei al party shared in the reign-

ing jealousy of Italy, and thought the safety of their own country demanded that they should prevent the establishment of a new Power which would be bound by gratitude, and perhaps by actual promises, join to iu the aggressive schemes of France. llow completely this notion is passing away may be seen from the explanation of motives published by 14 members of the Prussian Chamber who voted on the 6th instant against the Government, which they usually support. Some uneasiness prevailed yesterday in financial circles in Paiis in consequence of | unfavourable accounts received from Vien- j na with respect to Hungary and Dalmatia. There have not been any disturbances at Fiume, but the state of siege was declared because it was discovered that, notwithstanding the vigilance of the Austrian police, Fiuiue was the place of rendezvous (or the leaders of the Hungarian insurrection at home with those abroad. It is asserted that General Klapka, who was supposed to have remained constantly at Naples, was within the last month in the neighbourhood of the Adriatic. The pamphlet La France, Home, it Vltalie, of which I was enabled to send you copy a on Thursday, was issued here last night. The anonymous character of the publication is this time abandoned ; and the new manifesto of the Emperor Napoleon appears with a signature, that of come the Director of the Press, M. Laguerroniere. It is an elaborate defence of the Imperial policy in its relation to Italy and at the same time a regular bill of indictment against the Pope, or, officially speaking, the Papal Government It is criticized by the ultramontane journals, and, of course, highly approved by the Government press. I have alluded to the rumours about (lie Pope manifesting some intention of making concessions, and of trying by way of ex- j at periment the arrangements proposed by the Emperor of the French. Yet the reproachful tone of the present manifesto

goes far to weaken that supposition If there real ly were any chance of concessions of the kind from the Pope, the pamphlet would probably not have appeared ; or, if it did, it would have bestowed on his Holiness a fair share of the praises which are now reserved for his þÿ eldest þÿson. On the other hand , some persons are of opinion that La France, Rome, it Vltalie is meant ns the finishing stroke to the þÿPope s temporal authority ; that with all its assurances of respect and devotedness to the Holy Father, it is like the prime Havanriah cigar which Ferdinand VII. of Spain, with bland and apparently sincere expressions of affection, used to off r to the Minister or General whose disgrace he had just resolved upon ; and that the Emperor will let him drop with the same display of sympathy There King Naples. of shown is, to indeed, the fugitive in the last page of the pamphlet an assurance to the contrary, but I fear it is from that very assurance that over-suspicious and incredulous people draw their conclusions. þÿ In the þÿmeantime, says the exponent of Imperial policy, þÿ þÿ And in spite of all that hits occurred, in spite of so many refusals of the generous intervention of France, in spite of so much injustice, which have not exhausted his devotion, the Emperor, we are convinced, will leave his sword at Koine to insure the safety of the Holy Father. Faithful to his double duty of Sovereign elected by the national will, and ot eldest son of the Church, he cannot sacrifice Italy

to the Court of Rome, nor give over the Papacy to the Revolution. Impassible as the conscience and the right of a great people, he will await with patience the not distant hour when the Pontifical Government, disabused at last in the dangerous allies who have imposed their support on him, will know how to distinguish between those who have done all to destroy

T « C W 0 l! X KV l him and those who have done all to save þÿhim. This would ind icate that the large French forces now in possession of the Roman territory will remain there' some time longer. COMMUNICATION. To the Editor of the Airis, Sir! Witnessing what has been going on for a we> k or two at the Protestantkey, where a number of men under the direction of the Sergeant of the Fort are busy making the necessary preparations for mounting one of the three heavy guns which came out here a few years ago, (the others having just been sent down to West End for the same purpose,) one might he led to suppose that we had no less cause than our lellow-citizens in the mother country (whom we know are just now threatened with an attack by the Germans,) to prepare for war. That however, to the best of my knowledge, is far from being the case, and were it even otherwise, might we even be under appreheusiou of a visit from an enemy, I think it is pretty generally understood that it would be little short of madness to attempt any resistance against regular ships of war. Even against a privateer, which of course would bo armed with far-reaching guns of the very latest construction, we would stand, l am afraid, but a poor chance. The houses in town would be knocked about our ears without our being able with our old out-of-the-way guus to do her the least harm in return. The best constructed guus, and however great their number, would nevertheless bo but of little, if of any, use to us as a means of defence if the Island were attacked by a regular naval force, if only for the reason that all our supplies arc to he conveyed to us from abroad. Yet I will adiuit there might be opportunities where a couple of well directed

shots might be applied most effectually, provided they were fired from guns at least a match to tho.-e of our opponent. Accordingly I would not consider it a useless expense if some of the old guns belonging to the fort here were replaced by a couple of new ones, constructed on the most improved plan of late inventions ; and if the guns that were received here the other year had been such ones, I would think that nothing could be reasonably objected to their being sent out : but as they are þÿ old, worn-out-guns of many years standing, and much heavier in weight than is requisite (guns of the improved construction with their other advantages also joining that of being much lighter in weight than the old ones proportionally) I confess I cannot but consider the pilichase and sending out of such cannon at a cost of more than a thousand dollars a most inconsiderate outlay of the public money þÿ an outlay that I do not see how it can be justified to the taxpayers of this Island, and I think it rather surprising that the Government, instead of treating tliose old guns according to their merit viz : as so many pieces of useless metal, (and 1 am confident that for all practical purposes they cannot be viewed otherwise) are now haviug them mouuted, thereby incurring another outlay of public money, the usefulness of which T am

eiojo » ii afraid but few, if any, will he able to see ; and adding ano her comparatively laige item under the head of milituiy expences, þÿ an item which for the mounting o..ly of the cannon at the key uo doubt will come to a sum not far from $5oO. Your Obt. Servt. X

To the Editor of the Avis. Sut, Deeply convinced of the necessity for commenting upon the letter fiom the Burgher Council to the Govern r, as also of the good results to be derived from a thorough discussion upon the very important objects contained in tiiis letter, the writer of this will ask for some space in your paper, and hopes not to be refused this, aliliougli lie in no way concurs in the opinion and sentiments expn ssed by you in your editorial remarks preceding the publication of the letter. Sir, an editor of a newspaper lias in every country of the world certain social duties to he ruled by, the principal one of which consists in being, as circumstances may direct it, either the loader of public opinion, or its mouthpiece. In countries with laige populations, freedom of speech and of the press, where journalism lias attained rank as a power iu the Slate, the e the position of the press is easily defined wiiliin t he boundaries prescribed to each journal þÿby the political or other piiueiples of its own public, or rather, pirty; and the editor cannot transgress these boundaries, he cannot change what is called the colour of his journal, without incurring a punishment severer than nur press-laws can inti ct, viz : the loss of his public. But, in a small Island with a scant population, and having only one newspaper, which is ha dly read by the one-hundredth part of that population, there the position of that newspaper becomes very diffeient indeed I do not speak

of press-laws and censorship, which coudetnnable certainly, are not necessarily obstacles io a candid and free expiession ot sentiments; hut 1 mean to say, that in this small Island, filled with nothing hut differences as to its population, differences in races, nationalities, creeds, social stations, and political opinions, a population which has nevet possessed a public spirit, and consequeui ly no public opinion, there the press, that is its one single newspaper, cannot possibly repres nt one party only, it must give expression io facts which occur, and to ihe serf. us impressions and sentiments which they produce on and elicit from the people. In other words, Sir, your paper cannot, from the circumstances of your public, become the leader here of public opinion, but it ought to be its mouthpiece. As such it can effect a great deal of good, more so, in fact, llian by trying to form and shape public opinion, iu which, even with the gie>iesi editorial taleutl, it could never succeed ; hut, as such, it must be Ciuilous and impartial, it must deal fairly with all parties, it must give expression to the different opinions of people, but it should not adopt and express any of these conflicting opinions as its own, and thereby in a manner stamp them as expressions of the public opinion, without having first heard the opinions of other parlies on the subject in question, »nd having thoroughly siudied the subject-matter iu all its points and bearings. 1 have been 'led to this preamble, Sir, by a

profound conviction that you have lately as editor followed a wrong path. In your impression of the 5ih of this month, you supported a þÿ Protest from a þÿburgher, uud in your succeeding No., when shewn how wrong was this protest, you yet coutiuued, not only to support it, but. eveu to declare its contents to be the voice of public opinion. In this you were wrong, Sir, very wrong; public opinion, when in a normal sound state, would never countenance the abominable tendencies of the said protest. It is all tight that you should luseit it, and it is but natural that the people should drsiie the abolition of exorbitant fees and give expression to ihe desire, so far all right; but when you, instead ol simply inserting the protest, become its advocate, and try to prove its correctness by deducing it upon phiases of the most unblushing Communism, theu, Sir, y. u attempt to form a public opiuiou iu the matter, instead of listening io the seutiuients of others, and you go in a direction where your eulightened pubtio will never follow you.

So in your last publication. The contents of the þÿBurgher-Couucil letter s t o the Governor, you preface with your declarations not only of your own entiie adhesion, but of your hope that it will have the almost unanimous concurrence and support of the community, and which as a step in the right direction, you hope to see followed up by the Council etc. etc. etc. Now, I think, Sir, and I am very sure, many think with me, that you are vastly in advance of public opinion here upon the said letter and its merits, nay, 1 even think, that had you waited a little while, you would ere long have heard and read very different sentiments f oin those expressed by you, and you would have found a very genera) opinion in the Island set in the exact opposite dir cti n from that taken by the Burgher-Council, and so warmly lauded by you. Take tny word for it, Sir, and lie more waiy hereafter, you will lose nothing Ly waiting to hear the public scniimeut, instead ol anticipating it I shall, with your permission, begin iny humble comment upon the famous letter of the Buigln r-Council in your next number. I.\AUGI ISAL ADDRESS Of THE HE ABRAHAM LIMN, President of the united states. Delivered at Washington , March 4, 1861. Fellow -Citizens of the United States þÿ In compliance witli the custom of the old United States Government itself, 1 appear before you to address you briefly and take in your pr. sence the oath prescribed by ihe constitution of the United States to be tak. n by tbe Piesident before lie enters upon the execution of his office. I do not consider it necessary at present for me to discuss those matters of the Administration about which there is no specia. anxiety or excitement. Apprehension appears to exist among the people of the Southern States that by the aeces-ion of a Republican Administi ation their property, their peace, and their personal seeui ity are to be endangered. There has never been any reasonable c«n-e for such apprehension ; indeed, the most ample evidence to the contrary lies all the while existed and been open to tli eir inspection. It is found in neatly all the published speeches of liim who now addresses you. I do but quote f.cm one of those speeches when 1 d, clare that "I have no purpose, directly or indir.ctly, to inierfeie with the institution of slavery in the States whete it exists I believe I have no lawful right to do so, and 1 have uo inclination to do so." Those who nominated and elected me did s i with full knowledge that I had made this and many simian declarations, and n. ver recanted them ; and more than this, they placed in t lie

plutlorm, f..r my acceptance, and as a law to themselves, the clear and emphatic r> solution which I now read; the right ol States, and specially the right, of " Resolved, That the maintenance inviolate of . ea li State to order and cont.ol it- own dome-tic institutions according to its own judgitn nt, exclusively, is essential to that balance of the pow r on which the perfection and endurance of our own political labric depends, and we denounce the lawless invasion by armed foice, of the s il of any State or territory, no matter under what pietcxt, as among the gravest of ct imes." I now reiterate these sentiments, doing so only to press upon the public attention the most conclusive evidence of which the case is susceptible, that the piop. rty, peace and security of no section are to be, in any way, endangered by the now incoming Administration. I add, too, that all the protection which consistently with the constitution and the laws, can he given, will he cl.ecifuily given all States, when lawfully d. mantled, for whatever cause, gs cheerfully to one section as another. Thete is much controversy about dolivciing up fugitives Irom service or labor. The, clause 1 now read is as plainly written in the constitution as any other of i:s provisions : " No person, hi I I to service or labor in one State, under the laws thereof, escaping into another, shall, in consequence of any law or regulation thnein, be discharged Iront such service or labor, but shall be deliveted up, on claim of

the party to whom such service or labor may be due." It. is scarcely questioned that, this provision was intended, by those who made it, for reclaiming what we ca 1 fugitive slaves, and the intention of the law giver is the law, and all members of Congress swear their support to the whole constitution, to this provision as much as any otli. r. To the proposition, then, that slaves, wit. se cas s come within the terms of this clause, shall he deliveted up, their oaths are unanimous. Now, if til. y would make an effort in good temper, could they not, with nearly an equal unanimity, frame and pass a law, by means of which to keep good that unanimous oath ? There is some difference of opinion whether t his clause should be enforced by national or State authority, hut surely that difference is not a vety material one. Il a slave is to be surrendered it can he of hut little consequence to him or others by which authority it is done, and

should any one, in any case, be content, his oath shall go unk. pt on merely unsubstantial controversy. Ar.d here will rest the responsi- r bility. Again, in any law upon this subject, ought lized not all the saf, guards of humane jurisprudence be introduced, so liheity, known in civithat a free man be not, in any case, surrendered as a slave, and might it not be well at the same time to provide, by law, for the enforcement of that clause in the constitution which guarantees that the citizeus of each Slate shall be entitled to all the privileges and immunities of the citizens in the several States. I take the official oath to-day with no mental reservations, and with no purpose to construe the constitution or laws by any hypercritical rules, and while I do not chance now to specify particular acts of Congress as proper to be enforced, I do suggest that it will be much safer for all, both iu official and private stations, to conlortn to and abide by all those acts which stand unrepealed, than to violate any of them, trusting to find impunity in having them held to be unconstitutional. L is seventy-two years since the first inauguration of a President under the National constitution During that period fifteen different and I greatly d stinguished citizens have, in succession, administered the executive branches of the Government. They have conducted them through many perils, and generally with great success; yet, with all this scope for precedent, I now enter upon the same task for the brief consti-

tutional period of four years under great and pecu iar difficulties ; a disruption of the Federal Union heretofore only menaced, is now formally admitted. T hold that in contemplation of universal law, and the constitution, the Union of the States is perpetual. It is implied, if not expressed, in the fundamental law of national governments. It is safe to assert that no government proper ever had a provision in an organic law for its own termination. Continue to execute all express provisions, and our national constitution and Union will endure forever, it being impossible to destroy it, except by some action not provided for iu the instrument itself. Again, if the United States be not a government proper, hut an association of States in the nature of a contract merely, can it, as a contract, be practically unmade by less than all the parties who made it? One party to the contract may violate it, break it, so to speak, hut does it not require all to lawfully tescind it. Descending from these general principles, we find the proposition that in legal complication the Union is perpetual, confirmed by the history of the Union itself The Union is much older than the constitution. It was formed, in fact, articles of association in 1774. It was matured and enntb ued by the Declaration of Independence in 1776 Tt was further matured, and the faith of all the thirteen States expressly plighted and engaged that it should be perpetual by the articles of confederation in 1778, and finally in 17S7.

One of the declared objects for ordaining and establishing the constitution was to form a more perfect Union ; but if the destruction of the Uni. n by one or by part only of the States be lawfully possible, the Union is less perfect than before, the constitution having lost, its vital element of perpetuity. It follows from these views that no Slate, upon its mere motion, can lawfully go out of the Union; that resolves and ordinances to that effect are legally void ; that acts of violence within any State or States aeainst the authority of the United States are insurrectionary, or revolutionary according to circumstances. I therefore conside r that in view of the constitution and the laws, the Union is unbroken, and, to the extent, of my ability, I shall take care, as the constitution itself expressly enjoins upon roe, that the laws of the Union be faithfully ( xccuted in all the States. Doing this, I deemed it to be only simple duty en my part, atid I shall perform it, so lar as practicable, unless my rightful mastets, the American people, shall withhold the requisite means or in some authoritative manner direct the contrary. I trust, this will not l.e regarded as a menace, but only as the (lecl .rid purpose of the Union, that it will constitutionally defend and maintain itself. In doing this there need be no bloodshed or violence, and there shall he none, unless it be forced upon the national nuthoiity. The power confided to me will be used to hold and occupy and possess the property and places belonging
to the Government, and to collect duties on imports. But beyond what may be necessary for these objoots, there will be no invasion þÿ no using

of force against or among people anywhere. Where hosiiliiy to us, in any interior locality' shall be so great and so universal as to prevent competent resident citizens from holding the Federal offices, there will be no attempt to force obnoxious strangers among the people for that object. While the strict legal right may exist in the Government to use force to maintain these offices, the attempt to do so would be so irritating, and so nearly impracticable withal, that 1 deem it may be better to forego for the present the use ol such officers. The mails, unless repelled, will continue to be furnished to all parts of the Union so far as possible. The people everywhere shall have that sense of perfect security which is most favorable to calm thought and reflection. The course here indicated will be followed unless eurrent events and experience shall show modification or change to be prop, r, and in every case and exigency, my best discretion will he exercised accotding to circumstances actually existing, and with the fervent hope of a peaceful solution of the national troubles, and the restoration of fraternal sympathies and affection. There are persons in one section or another who are said to seek to destroy the Union at all events, and are glad lor any pretext to do it. I will neither affirm or deny that there be such. 1 need address no words to them. To those, however, who really love the Union, may I not speak? Before entering upon so grave a matter as the destruction ol our national fabric, with

all its benefits, memories and hopes, would it not be wise to ascertain precisely wiiy do it ? Will you hazard a desperate step while there is a possibility of any portion of the ills you fly from having no real existence f Will you, while certain the ills you fly to ate greater than all the real ones you fly from? Will you risk the commission ol so feaiful a mistake ? All profess to he content in the Uniou if all constitutional rights can be maintained. Is it true, then, that any right plainly written iu the constitution has been denied ? I think not. Ilappily, the human mind is so constituted that no party can reach to the audacity of doing this. Think, if you can, of a single instance in which a plainly written provision of the constitution has been denied ! If, by the mere force of numbers, a majority should deprive the minority of any clearly wiitten constitutional right, it might in a moral point of view justify revolution. It certainly would, if such a right were a vital one ; but such is not our case. AH the vital rights of minorities and individuals are so plainly assured them by affirmations and negations, guarantees and piohibitioos, in the constitution, that controversies never can arise concerning them. But. no organic law can ever he framed with provisions specifically applicable to every question which may occur in its practical administration. No foresight can anticipate, nor any document ot reasonable length contain expn ss provisions for all possible questions. Shall fugi-

tives from labor be surrendered by national or by State authority? The constitution does not expressly say May Congress prohibit slavery in the territories ? The constitution docs not expressly say. Must Congress protect slavery in the territories 1 The constitution does not expressly say. From questions of this class springs ail our constitutional controversies, and we divide upon them into majorities and minorities. If the minority will not ncquiesce, the majority must, or the government must cease. There is no other alternative for continuing it hut acquiescence on one side or the other. If tlio minority in such case will secede rather than acquiesce, they make a precedent which in time will divide and ruin them. For, a minority of their own will secede from them whenever a majoiity chooses to be controlled by such a minority. For instance, why may not any portion of the new Confederacy, in a year or two hence arbitrarily secede again, precisely as portions of the present Union claim to secede from it ? All who cherish disunion sentiments are now being educated to the exact temper of doing this. Is there such a perfe ct identity of infeiest among the States to compose the new Union as to produce harmony only and prevent renewed secession ? Plainly, the cential idea of seces-ion is the essence of monarchy. A majority, In Id in restruint by constitutional check and limitations, and always changing easily with ttie uelibeiute changes of popular opinions and sentiments, is

t iu only true sovereignty of a free people. Whoever rejects it does of necessity fly to anarchy or to despotism Unanimity is itnpo-sihle ! The rule of the minority, as a permanent arrangement, is wholly inadmissible, so that rejecting the majority, the principle of anarchy or despotism in some form is all that is left.

For a long while u heavy cloud has hung over our Island, loading its air, at it were, wiili an oppressive, almost a sickening sensation, checking its vital functions, and inspiring tearful misgivings and apprehensions ns of some unknown evil to befall us. This sensation, hko a kind of soci al malaria, lias been felt more or less lay ail in -mbers of this community, except Estate-laborers, whose happy lot exhibits a singular contrast to the troubles and miseries of the vest of the inhabitants, and except the Government. officials, whom their never failing salaries place beyond this infested atmosphere It is this oppressive feeling, this foreboding of coming evils, which, set king vent, has burst forth in the Burgher þÿCouncil s letter; and viewing it in this light, gives to the Council and their letter perhaps the only defence, or rather excuse, for being in every respect out of form, and out of order For iu this singular manifestation, the Burgher Council arrogates to itself the functions appertaining to the Colonial Council, and exceeds the limits prescribed for its sphere of action by the law of 9th May

proposals gher Council the Governor to Our privilege of milking þÿ as are considered tend- inch ing to Ike common interest of the municipality Now, the letter before us treats ou very differeut matters, and its proposals go far beyond the common municipal interest, and so tar it is out of the order established for the action of the Burgher Council. This may to some seem a mete matter of form, a breach ot form, it you will, but on the whole a mere trifle, not worth wasting words upon, when compared to the importance of the maiter and to the appropriateness of the measure. But this would be highly erroneous. The forms are just as much enacted by law, as the actions, ard a breach of a Burgher legal form is a breach ot the law. ns I he Council has not been instituted a political, Government-advising body, whereas the Colonial Council has been created expressly for this purpose, and it would not do for the firstnamed Council to usurp the attributes and (unctions of the latter. Were the Burgher Council to be countenanced in this way of acting, then it might as well transgress all and eveiy other rule in its fundamental ordinance, overturn all the landmarks between its own competency and that of the oilier established bodies, in short become revolutionary and creaie anarchy. This has clearly been far from the iutention of the Council, but it suggests itself upon a serious reflection ; and for that reason it must be presumed, t hat the Council, or perhaps individual inembei s thereof, have in the huny wit i

which the measure is known to have been urged through the Council, nottakui a sufli cient time for mature reflection upon the subject iti all its bearings. If brought forth in a Court ot law ns claim lor the plaintiff, it would be nonplused as coming from an incompetent part ; and it would give the authority to whom it is addressed an unul.j, clionahle plea for treating it as non avenue . It so, it would place the Burlead them on to other manifestations, and gher Council iu noiiiviable position, it might it might end in a rupture with Government, fail- in vain regrets and heartburnings, and in yet ing to biing about the least good i esult. And iijl of tins wou d be nw ng to the first fMse step. So necessa y is it, especially for all cotporate bodies, to move stiietly within the limits ascrih d to them by their charter. Besides this innate breach of fotm, vitiating, as I l ave shewn, the document nb origine, theie are in the lettei other sins against form, which with the queer st\le it is couched in, give to it a ludietou- soit of inc diet ence, and fatigues one in pet using it. As falling under this poition of tny commentary, l shall call particular att ntion to the following paragiaph in the Burgher þÿCouncil let- s ter : The Btirghei Council representing St. ' stances not in any respect be justified in þÿ Croix, would under the present, circutnþÿ þÿ awaiting either a new meeting of the Colo- nial Counci1, or any better results þÿthereof; etc ; and I would humbly ask, what do these words mean in common sense ? To the Editor of the St. Croix Avis. Silt ! An occurrence took place in St þÿJohn s Ch arch iu this Town on Saturday last, unparalleled in the annals of our community, or pe'rliaps of any other, and which in my opinion as well as others, calls for the atiimadveision of all right thinking persons þÿ the occurrence alluded to is this þÿ the appointed day for pet forming the rites Saturday the 23rd instant, being of baptism on the infants of parents attached to that Church, a number of these infants were canied to the baptismal font to receive the holy tite, when, strange to say, the Minister officiating, positively refused to perform the rites on eight or nine of these infants, on the ground of their illegitimate birth ! ! ! 1 leave your readets to imagine the harrowing feelings experienced by the Parents of the-e repudiated innocents, repudiated by the Minister ol God and performer of Hi holy ordinances from participation in a rite of the Church parti, ularly adapted for infants þÿ and for what? Because they were illegitimate þÿ illegitimate lotsooth ! Del the children make themselves illegitimate? Had they the smallest control over the manner in which they should be ushered into the world? I say thrice no! and if no, why should the sins of the fathers be visited on unoffending ininnts totally unconscious of the evils in which they were begotten? Our Lord and Saviour on rebuking his disciples, expressly says, þÿ Suffer little children to come unto me and lot bid them

not, for of such is the kingdom of þÿheaven. Our Saviour did not say, þÿ Suffer little legitimate children to come unto þÿme, for he would thereby have repudiated att incredible amount of illegitimate chi dren, swarms of whom must have existed at that period among Jew and Gentile, in consequence of polygamy being so prevalent among them. 1 would simply ask the Reverend Gentleman who performed this act of Christian charity on Saturday last, whether, if he had lived in the time of the Stuarts iu England and happened to be one of the Court Chaplains, ho would have refused the rite of baptism to the infant children of the too notorious Nell Guyun, tho Dutchess of Portsmouth &c. &c. who bore

illegitimate children to both Charles and James the 2nd? Nay nearer our own time if be would have refused the rite to the illegitimate progeny of William 4th ? I believe not, but no doubt the illegitimate Scions of royalty would iu the Learned þÿDivine opinion, s be worthy of regeneration by baptism, while the poor innocents of our Island are so much beneath his valuation of salvation, that he could ignomiuiously spurn them from the house prepared for the reception of þÿGod s children. I could say much more on the subject, but as
I am compelled to cease.

Yours, with regard, P. Q. Y. The public sentiment upon tlie subject of Slavery and the Slave Trade seems at last to have entered upon its rational and, as we may hope, its p, rmancut state. A hundred and fifty years ago we were fighting for the privilege of conveying Negioes over sea. Having obtain, d all we desired on tit at score, we then apathetically pocketed tlie piofits, and positively refused to think of how those profits wire obtained. A g. iteration later and we gtew uncomfortable in our gains, and our ears tingled and our coiiscieii'-es gr w uneasy as the wails and groans of tlie st,il d Negroes canto home to us writ pe petual aud importunate repetition. We were some years awak ning, and Wilberloice and Claikson, and all the lellow-labourers of these men, had much to do thoroughly to arouse us nut of that uneasy state of somnolence. But at Iasi we did awake, aud we awoke in a Ireiizy Tlie state of this country when the full guilt ol Slavery came upon it was nothing less than a fr« nzy of remorse. B fore that passion everything w, lit down. Many men yet living can remember when George Canning failed to obtain as a concession the abolition of tit.- p wor to flog female slaves, and young men can remember when it was thought litile less than blasphemy to sugg st that even a black man might very reasonably be expected to do some labour. Beiween the-e two extremes the public seiiiitneni has violently vibrated. In the paroxysm of his first remorse the gttihy English-1

tnan saw Slaveiy iu everything hlark. The phantom of that C"fnplaining Negro was ever before him, and he would shut his eyes and scream if you did hut talk to him of a Negro at work. He sacrificed everything to his sore, quivering conscience, lie was ever upon the watch t' find out something more to saciifice. He saeiificed his great West Indian interest not only recklessly, hut with an ostentatious eagerness. He east his own twenty millions down to rid hiuiseli of the remaining evidences of liis ctime ns peniteutly as Judas i ffered the thiity pieces of silver to the Jewish authorities. He poured forth not only his own money and the money of those over whom he held iufluence,

but he lavished the life of his own kith and kin to appease that accusing conscience. On the coast of Africa, in the perfidious sunshine of þÿ the white þÿmau grave," s amid the beatttilul and deadly luxuriance of a tropical vegetation, he placed b is own countrymen to pine and die that he might comfort himself with the satisfaction that he had atoned for the great siu he had committed against the black man. For a full generation there was nothing he would not pay, and nothing be would not vicariously endure. Every great excitement has its recoil. The generation of crime had been followed by the generation of temorse; the generation of remorse is followed by the generation of reflection. We who uo at occupy the earth are less affected by the crimes of our grandfathers or the remorse of our fathers. We begin to leel less affright at th is spectre of the writhing Negio. We have purged ourselves completely of the guilt of his abduction and his other wrongs, and we can feel ourselves entitled to look upon him as we might look upon any other man who has succeeded to the common obligation of eating bread by the sweat of his brow. The flood tide, which had flowed upwards, roaring and foaming like the þÿ bore ot some bell-shape 1 firth, retained its power of flowing after the great impulse had ceased; hut years ago there were some who ventured to say that,; alter all, the earth must be tilled, and that the great law of Nature which doomed mau to labour must apply to the black man as well as to the white. Their voices,

however, had little chance of being heard, fur there was enough of vehemence iu our old convictions to urge us not only to persuade but to coerce all the lest of the world to feel as we felt and to be penitent as we were peniteDt. We lavished our money, we concentrated our efforts, we exerted all our influence, we compromised our political relations, we coerced the weak, and we went to the verge of making war upon the strong, in order to bring the rest of the world to joiu with us in our orusade against the traffic in mankind. Never was there in the history of our race so magnificent and so disinterested an enthusiasm. When the gr< at book of history shall become so vast that far-off generations shall be unable to seize any other than the tallest events in the great vista from which they emerge, this woik of England must stand out and challenge admiration, us simething to which the story of past ages has no parallel. We English alone have hern hearty in the cause. We have shamed some hy our example, we have bought others by our largesses, and we have deterred others, by our power; but of all the peoples of the earth we alone have laboured, with gold and with aims, for no other object than for that point of conscience which is to u9 our þÿ idea þÿ to put down Slavery and the Slave Trade. Yet we have not succeeded. While we have been starving our own colonists and suffering our West Indian possessions to return to jungle in very fanaticism, suspecting that Slavery must lurk under every

contract for labour, other countries have eluded their engagements or have openly resented our interference. Portugal has required all our attention to keep her at all up to the mark ; Spain has impudently repudiated all her promises; France has changed the name, but not the substance ; and America has continued the odious traffic at sea under the pretext of a jealousy of her national honour, and has, to her misfortune, nursed Slavery at home and acknowledged it as a domestic institution. After all our sacrifices and all our efforts the most zealous opponents of Slavery were fain to come down to the House of Commons on Tuesday night, and to propose a resolution, þÿ That the þÿ meanshitherto employed by this couutry for the suppression of the African Slave Trade þÿ, have tailed to accomplish that object. þÿ Now that we can calmly review all that has been done we find that we have been led away by our generous impulses and have wasted our strength uselessly. Like the charge at Balaklava, þÿ (Test tnugnifique, mais ce nVst pas la þÿ guerre; þÿ it was wonderful, but it was altogether unpractical. Great as we are, we arc Dot powerful enough to coerce the world. Strong as wc arc, we must submit to the laws which universally influence human conduct. After all our vain efforts we are reduced at last to admit that we must be oootent to attract mankind by their interests, and not pretend to govern them by fear. France claps her hand upon her sword if we presume to ask whether

% ft 0- B. D I. tf I she has slaves or free labourers in the hold of the Cbarles-et-Georges. Spain laughs at us if we pretend to prevent her from importing as many slaves as she may want in Cuba. America threatens war if we attempt to liberate the live cargo of a vessel covered with the stars and stripes. We have discovered at last that commercial competition will do what fleets and armies are utterly incompetent, to perforin Not very long ago, when we, from time to time, urged the claims of our West Indian colonies to some substituted free labour for the slave labour they had lost, we were met by the indignation of our Anti-Slavery Societies Perhaps there at e some remnants of that superstition, which is a great religion degenerated, wherein the same dogmas are still repeated; but on Tuesday night the modern Anti Slavery men came down to ask the House of Commons to beþÿ lieve that þÿ in countenancing immigration into countries the true remedy is to he found, not þÿ where Slavery exists, but io augmenting the þÿ workingpopulation in countiies in which þÿ þÿ failure has mainly arisen from our having Slavery has been abolished þÿ; and þÿ that the þÿ endeavoured almost exclusively to prevent þÿ the supply of slaves, instead of to check the þÿ demand for þÿthem. At last we are condesoeuding to reason upon Slavery and the Slave Trade as wo reason upon other hutnau affairs At last wo are coming down from our high ootions of destroying everything we do not like by the sword and the cannon-shot þÿ although

there are some fanatics, as the Debate showed, who still lean upon these means þÿ and are intent on humbling ourselves to the commonplace notion that the best þÿway of destroying an objectionable system of labour is to undersell it. Africa, populous as it is, is not so populous as China, nor is it so populous as the coast of India. Africa, nec ssitous as the people may he, is not so nere-sitous as the Far Ea-t. There we have a hungry civilization which may be moulded to our purposes hy good treatment more cheaply than the savagery of Africa can be oppressed hy coercion. Both in India and in China wc have the materials lor a competition which may render the Slave Trade an extinct, because an unprofitable, traffic. The old Anti-Slavery Party will probably for some time still oppose all white emigration, lest it should compel their free black proteges to work hy the compctiiiun that emigration most create iu the labour-maiket; but we are happily getiing beyond tliis stage of folly, and ure learning to o< k upon this subject wi<h ilia eyes of common seu-e. We have a treaty with China which enables us to carry to the West not only Chinamen but their families. We have behaved so well to them that we have gained their confidence. While other nations may kidnap them Lv tens, we can obtain volunteers by thousands; and if our laws are observed, and our shipowners and planters are honest, we are not far fioin the period when we may see the prosp rity of our West Indian colonies restored and the Slave
Trade extinguished without a cruiser or a foil on the coast of Africa, and without the saciifice of even another million from t lie British Treasury

The þÿHtii'Kliei -Coiiiieil Letter. s Continued from No. 25 It is quite true that comprehensive reforms arc urgently wanted in several branches of the administration of this Island, in the administration of the Government and of Justice, fully as much a> in the economical mattcis, and this truth cannot but be acknowledged by all, Government itself probably not excepted. To bting about such reforms should be the steady An article in your last number signed þÿ Anti- aim of the inhabitants through their competent representatives, and if this were done in the right way, in a legal and constitutional manner, there can be liaidly a doubt but that the reforms solicited by the general public voice would be granted. But, to attain this cud, it is absolutely necissary to adopt none but strictly leg.il means, and to proceed in a different manner from the Burgher-Council. For although, as 1 have said, there is much iu their letter which, in a general way must be agreed to as expressing the sense of the public ou these matters, ytt has the Burgher-Council no title and no l ight to be the spokt small thereof ; and let not this be. pronounced a mere legal quibble, for that body does not represent St. Croix, and this fallacy, twice though ass. rted in their letter, does not change their legal position and functions from being admiuistrato<s to the municipality, to those of being representatives of the Island, nor could the Bland and the Government acknowledge them as such. In plain

words, the Burgher-Council represents nothing hut the municipality strictly so called, whilst þÿEpiscopalian the Colonial-Council represents the Island as part of the Colony, and this essential distinction, founded in common sense as well us in the true principles of polity, and enacted by luw, remains in full force, and cannot be subverted by ever so many highsouiiding phrases of the municipal cot porulioii, proclaiming their impatience for a new meeting of the Colonial- Council, and in the same breath their want of confidence in the results thereof. The Burgher-Council, then, does not much value the Colonial-Council, and this avowal certainly coincides with the gcneial, I may almost say the uuauimous, sentiment in the Colony. But, for all that, the institution is yet extant, and be its existence ever so drowsy and consumptive, yet while it lasts, it must serve. Nor can it be denied all possibility of being made to serve, if used in the tight way, and given a fair chance. This has as yet never been the case, nor will it ever be, unless the public be allowed to have a voice through their votes at the polls, which, as everybody knows, has most unfortunately never been the case here. We have well defined electoral laws, liberal, and based ou a moderate franchise, yet we have no bona fide free elections, the I'r, edom of electing being to the contrary repressed till it is almost unknown, and the representatives are mere nominees of half a dozen planters or attorneys to absent planters, who generally vote them-

selves in. With this abuse of electiotieeiing, which has now become systematic here, it is impossible that the Public should feel any ioterest either in the elections, or in the doings of the Council, which have both become matters of the utmost indifference ; and with this feeling, it is of course incompatible for the Public to raise its voice, and to make it heard and respected. But to those who know aught of the constitusistant clergyman should be sent for, or, th þÿ tional regime, of its life-inspiriting vigour, of

the healthy energy on the hustings, and of the stiength which the approval of his constituents confers upon the þÿelected, and many of those I here address are born and brought up under the freest constitution in all the world, and therefore ought to know it, þÿ to those, I say, I need not point out how absolutely indispensible is the public voice to support and strengthen the elected ones. Without it, what can the representatives do? Without it, where are the energy, the power, the influence, which we see carry all things before them when derived front a free election, founded upon the free and unshackled public voice ? Alas, they are not. there. It is like a tree cut off by its roots and suspended in mid-air, its fruits cannot ripen, they become blasted and are cast away. Herein lies undoubtedly the key to much of the failure of the Colonial-Council, and to the small sympathy and regard felt for it geneially. Our five or six nabobs, neither wisely nor Weil, ordering their dependents to vote and whom to vote for, outnumbei ing and suppressing all other voters, and so having none but themselves and their friends elected, they have brought dislike and discredit upon the institution ; and just as tiny have made it a tool for their own purposes, so they should not be sui prised on finding the Government adopt the same manoeuvre, and make use of tlm Colonial-Council in a like manner; for the Government, whether here or at home cannot be expected to pay much d.ference to a body debased by its

own incmbcis in their election. And the same thing occurs with the Burgher- Council, and carries with it the same icsttlt. Theie too, the numbers are nominated, not elected, and there too, prevui.s no public voice, and dwel s little ol public sympathy atrd nguid. Add to this its internal discords, its blunders, its reckless appropriations of the public turds to tbe private uses of its members, while measures the most beneficial aud of tbe most urgent neces-ity are postponed ad mlendas gracas for the want of these same funds, add too, the sovereign contempt in which it holds its so-called constituents, along with its responsibility toward them, and there would appear tlr po-sibility of a doubt, whether the Public might wish, with the Editor of this paper, to go so far in their appreciation of the merits of the Burgher-Council, as to give it a public testimonial of þÿ concurrence and þÿsupport. I crave pardon for imputing blunders to the honorable Burgher-Council, hut I affirm that no disrespect is meant thereby, blunders originating in error of judgment, or in weak powers of thought, and tin se defects being not subject, to our dominion. But I cannot help rigarding their letter and yet more its publication, ns a very great blunder indeed. We suffer from want ol credit, wc complain of the Banks as well as private hunkers and merchants closing their put si strings, and we strain every nerve to obtain barely the most necessary means for carrying ou our business ; yet we see the Council,

our would-be representative, going out of its ordinary course, and taking pains to proclaim in the most efficient way in its reach, our insolvency, our accumulation of arrears, our exhaustion of credit, our desperate situation. Is this very prudent ? I> it le.-s injurious, than when a few months ago a piivate individual from here, it was said, caused us serious harm by preaching the same homilies in St. Thomas? What an outcry we raised against that individual, what hard names we applied to him, had we had the power, he would have been stoned or crucified ; ami then what a sin upon our heads, tor was he more guilty or less innocent thau our conscript fathers, who uow so ampiy testify to his words ? Far better would it have been for the credit of the community, for tbe dignity of the Council, and for the attainment of a desirable result, if the Council had let alone the publication of their letter, and iu truth, the letter itself too, and if instead thereof, they had asked the inhabitants to sign an unanimous address to Government, calling for a speedy convocation of the Colouial-Council, and hud they then presented their piop' sals to this Council. But it is not too late to do so, in fact the convocation is resolve d upon ; and the Colouial-Council being about to be assembled witldn five or six weeks, the occasion presents itself to tbe Burgher- Council to improve upon its act by now proposing to the inhabitants for their sign-

ing, a petition or address to the Colonial -Council, embodying the proposals in their letter, hut stating them with more distinctness and in a more detailed manner, than in said letter, where every statement and every cipher is taken on trust, instead of being substantiated by vouchers or indisputable calculations. In this manner Fate befriends the Burgher-Council, and helps it, with a little discretion and good will of its own, out of an embarrassing position, easier than it could reasonably have hoped for. And the author hereof will willingly contribute his weak efforts to analyse the several multi rs proposed by the Council, and to put them in their proper light, humbly praying that his good will may be taken tor the deed and atone for the errors he may commit in lecturing upon schemes so vast and ill-defined as these shadowed forth in the þÿBurgher-Council P s roposals. Washington, March 13, 1861 Information has just been received in this city of the most important character from Montgomery. The Southern administration know that the evacuation of Forts Sumter and Pick ns has been decided on. Despatches from General Beauregard, represent that it would be utterly impossible for any united force that the administration at Washington could collect, to prevent the surrender of Major Anderson before the lapse of many weeks. Despatches from Washington have also assured the Montgomery government that no attempts at reinforcement will be made, and that the troops of the United States will be soon withdrawn. President Davis has, however, received the most ominous enmmunication8 from his friends here, respecting the intentions of the Lincoln administration to blockade Southern ports, and mako an attempt to collect the revenue. He is assured that the

Senator þÿDouglas Effort to Ascertain the Policy of the President, Washington, March 13. 1861. The introduction of the resolution of Senator Douglas, calling upon the administration for in-

. formation respecting the forts and other property within the limits of seceding States, is variously interpreted by republican Senators. His idea is to get at the intentions of the administration, with the hope of developing its policy, and show that it is one of peace. If the resolution is adopted, it will give the President an opportunity to state that he has no power to execute the laws, collect the revenue, or even to protect the public property, and that until Congress clothes him with that power it will be impossible for the government to make war upon any of the seceding States. Senator Douglas will sustain his resolution in a speech, iu which he will declare that it is the duty of the administration to pursue a peace policy. He will show that þÿ ties among the republicans a peace party, a war there are three parparty, aud a third party, who are neither one thing nor the other, who are for pursuing that sort of shilly-shally, namby-pamby policy which, if cariied out, must result in utter ruin to the country, aud a general prostration of all our commercial and other interests. The resolution is a step in the right direction. The administration are evidently without any fixed policy in regard to affairs in the South, for they are changing front nearly every day. One thing is certain, they are greatly embarrassed, aud would gladly take advantage of any chauce of extrication.

Startling News from Washington. It will be seen, by reference to our telegraphic despatches from Washington, that the preparations which are being made in the navy yards of the North, for aggressive attempts to collect the revenue, aud to throw troops into Forts Jefferson, Taylor and Pickens have created the deepest aud most intense excitement, at the capital of the Southern confederacy. The surrender of Fort Sumter is regarded as having been a necessity, and not a peace offering The intelligence, however, that a blockade was about to be attempted, coupled with the threats contained in President þÿLiu:oln inaugural, s is credited, and the most strenuous efforts are being made to forestall hostile action, by mustering an army which shall at once march upon Washington, if the coercive schemes of the administration are perse vored iu. President Davis is convinced that no objection would be made to the transit of an army through the border States ; hut that the people of Virginia and Maryland, would, on the contrary, rally to his support; and reinforce his ranks. With the first notification of hostile acts upon the Southern coast, the troops of the confederacy will march, and then will be seen the þÿ beginning ot the þÿend of the dreadful national drama enacting in the country. It is no time for General Scott to leave Washington now. His services there may be soon needed. Neither is the summons of General Wool for one hundred thousand men, to aid in defending the seat of government, to he now

regarded as unreasonable. þÿ Battle, which Mr. Seward declared might be the last resort in the present crisis may he near at hand, and tho safety of Mr. Lincoln in the White House, may soon depend, either upon his desisting from the course which he and his advisers are pursuing, upon flight, or upon the most formidable preparations for defence that can be collected together.

VV E have published in our columns several communications tending on the ill-advised and unjust measure of the Rector of St. þÿJohn c s hurch, in refusing to baptize illegitimate children. We will not question the motive on his part wh eh has led to this measure. It may be a good one; and may originate in a mind highly enthusiastic in þÿGod w s ork. But let not evil be done that good may come. The causes cf illegitimacy are not confined to this Island, nor to the West Indies, but have a world wide existence. Surely the Rector of St. þÿJohn s cannot expect to find among a population, two-thirds of which have just emerged from the soul-debasing curse of slavery, that morality, and those virtues, which centuries of civilization and liberty have failed to produce in Europe? The flag of Spain substituting that of the late Republic under a salute of one hundred and one guus. Geucral Santana, the late President, would, in the name of Her I Most Catholic Majesty, hold the appointment of Csptain-Geueral of the Province. A very important decree had also been published calling iu all the late Government paper money in circulation, and the terra of one year was fixed for its final withdrawal, and to be received at the exchange of $-1,000 paper for one doubloon, or sixteen dollars in gold. It is stated that this sudden and untoward change in the Government had been effected without any unfavorable result, g' and to the time of the departure of the schooner tranquillity was said to prevail everywhere. (Concluded ) I shall not follow the Council through their essays on taxation, in which they are seeu with astounding facility to jump over every obstacle, and to jump with equal ease at their conclusions. Neither will I stop nt their military tattle, passing by even their admiiahle inutualprotection-theory, þÿ police to protect us, military to protect police ; þÿ 1 am, in truth gettiug

tired'of the commonplaces and the truisms and the conclusions on trust, in which the letter abounds þÿ I -hall only repeat, that what few really useful hints may be found spread over the letter, are there in a merely raw state, requiring elucidations and discussions before they could he used. But let us for a moment suppose, thatevery body agreed in all respects with the Burgher-Council, and that in admiration of their letter, the competent authority would tell them : " go and do these things just as y"U have said what a stew the Council would then bo iu. Tbe Secretary's office is already puiged of its superabundant nuisances, and is consequently vastly more effective. We now think of falling too to reduce arid rearrange our taxes, and to effect a financial separation between tbis Island and the sister Islands, next between this Island and Denmark. In the meantime, all the chests are empty, and every body is crying out for money ; the Buigher-Cuuncil's fiist step in its higliinightiucss being of course to share out the Landlreasuiy among tire indigent planters, the

Council's own scribe taking no less than a third thereof for his own share, and its chairman probably another slice But there is no money forthcoming ; nobody thinks of paying taxes, and all who depended for tln-ir livelihood upou the hundreds of soldiers, officeis and officials Si nt away, they are now destitute, they may posse s houses, hut they cannot pay taxes tlicieon. The circulation of money is largely diminished, incomes are reduced, and in many cases wholly swept away ; nothing hut despair and a sullen silence. Then, the Burgher-Council perceives that it pos-e-ses neither the ability nor the attainment- in ces-ary for legislating and least of all, for rearranging taxation ; its scribe has fish of his own to fry, and having got what lie aimed at, lie leaves tin- Council in the lurch ; and lastly the Government must step iu to relieve the Council and put it hack again in its own wonted splietc. The letter further hints at reforming the present system which tends to centralize all legislative and administrative action in Copenhagen ; and this is one of the most useful hints in ilia letter, which if rightly developed to its legitimate consequences, will hare for result the reestahlishuiciit of the former Koyal Couucil acting with a Governor, and etrjoyiug collectively a much cu!a>gcd sphere ot action and power. But how this measure should tend to save expenditure, I at least cannot sec. 1 have already stated, as my opinioD, that there are at the moment two objects to which

any petition from Itcie should be limited, viz: tin- unconditional abolition of the double export duty, and the gi anting of an ample loan for immigration purposes. The double duty I have always considered so unjust and unjustifiable, that no equivalent ought to be baigairicd for in abiogating it. And 1 am glad to find from the Governor's reply to the, Burgher-Council's letter, that there is a hope ol seeing this matter speedily adjusted. The second object may prove more difficult, hut not the less desirable, of obtaining, and iu common justice as in good policy D, nma.k ought to assist us therein. Even on these terms it might he difficult enough to raise a private loan ; theielore let us petition the proper authorities to lend us this money from the Oresunds-Fund, which consisting now of many Millions invested at a lower rato of interest, might with so much better grace spare u- this slender part thereof as a loan, as the Colonies in .i t I claim to have a part in the Fund i seif, and nng' expect i his part to he. invested in the C .inert.
