To the Editor of the. St. Croix Avis. Sir, Arising, no doubt, out of the agitation which has been lately got up in reference to some matters relating to the affairs of the English Church in this town, I have heard many strange remarks ma'le with regard to the position of the English Episcopal Church in this Island, which leads roe to the conclusion that many persons not only belonging to the Church, but. others, have no very definite idea whether the church in this Island is under the supervision of the church in England, or that of the church in America, or. in fact, whether there don't exist a sort of mixed authority of both. One gentleman indeed, went so far not long since, when the Rectorship ot St. John's Church was vacant, as to express his opinion that an English Clergyman never would suit the congregation" It might be asked was he afraid that such an one would deal

tf , CROIX A v II, loo tenderly with the pet vices of the people in order to gain popularity ? Perhaps so. With the view therefore ot setting lltose right who may not be well informed on the subject, 1 beg permission to offer a few j observations touching this matter. I It is undeniable that frum the very beginning tiie church was established in this Island upon the foundation of lite national Church in England, and was so admitted and recognised by t he Danish Government, and has ever since been maintained on the footing of establishment. And it is equally undeniable that, the church here, as was þÿ case also in all the British Colonies at the time was | the considered to be under the ecclesiastical Jurisdiction of the Bishop of London, to whom was referred all questions pertaining to its affairs ; which was continued until the period of the appointment of Bishops in the West Indies. Referring to this important event, and the epoch which it marks in the history of the church in the West Indies, as well as its connection and influence with respect to the isolated and peculiar position ot the church hero, I must particularly bring to notice, that while Bishop Coleridge was the guest of General von Sohnlten, on his fir,-t visit at the seat of Government in this Island, his Excellency took occasion, while presenting the Vestries ot both Churches " Gentlemen to this distinguished prelate, emphatically to remark þÿ minds of this is the head of youb church, who is recognised by His Majesty the King of Den-
mark. and whom you are to obey in ale si'ihitual þÿmatters" or words to this effect, as near as living witnesses can recnllect.

But, to resume the thread of my remarks, it is to be stated furthermore, that for very many years no clergyman ever held the incumbency "f the church here but sucli as were ordained in England, and this order of things continued down to the close ol the Ministry of that most excellent Divine, the Reverend Itohert Adams. A little in advance of which period, it must be observed, a church edifice had been erected in West End, under the denomination ofSl Paul's, and a separate clergyman was employed for the performance of the regular dmies of that parish, where previously the people belonging to the church in that locality had only occasional services afforded them by the Rector of St. John's, who usually visited them at stated periods, or when particularly called fur. Subsequent to the period here indicated, the condition ot both churches suffered under many trying and unpleasant vicissitudes, tiie causes of winch it might be more instructive tlian Hgreeahle to trace or describe, when scenes were enacted, and worthy and zealous clergymen were often used in a way winch charity might wish to cover, bill which truth must not always hide. But as the occurrences here but slightly alluded to, are yet so near to us, þÿ still in the recollection of most people particularly ami must be about West End, it would answer no purpose ol the writer uf these remarks to entpr into a detail of circumstances, or to awaken unpleasant feelings hi the breasts of some of the actors in tho church Cabals

which were formerly so common in tiiat quarter; and who, I regret to perceive by way of keeping their hands in, as it would appear, are at lln» present time meddling in the affairs of a neighbouring church with which they have no concern, t his aiding to fan the flames of dissension which, but lor their u mailed lor interference had not certainly reached its present dimensions. Returning however, from tins short digression. it must be stated that during the course of several years, the Pulpits of both churches were very irregularly supplied with Ministers, and, from whatever cause it may have arisen, it was not always practicable to obtain tiie services of English ordained Ministers; hut without stopping to enquire how, or why this was so, it brings us to the important fact, that about tins period commenced the practice of þÿ what was t lien admitted tu be a pressing necessity employ- þÿ ing American ordained clergymen, amongst whom, be it said, were several talented, pious, and pxemplary men. Is it not, therefore, obviously plain from the manner in winch the congregations were thus compelled to supply themselves with clergymen against one of the most stringent rules of the church in England, that neither the rules, or t'aiions (framed 300 years ago for a church very differently situated to ours) by which the church is sustained in England, could at all times be acted upon, or made applicable to our peculiar circumstances here 1 Mad these rules been adhered to, no American ordained Minister could

have been permitted to preach in an English Episcopal church, much less to hold the appointment of Rector. For what is there to render it obligatory on a clergyman of the American Anglican church to be governed by the Canons of the church of England of which the King (or Queen) is the supreme head, whom lie don't acknowledge ? Hoping this brief outline of a subject whicli is capable of being much more enlarged upon, may lie nselul in showing the futility, at least ot so much talk upon all occasions about " the þÿCanons" and I trust will leave no doubt on any one's mind regarding the foundation of the church in this Island. In regard to tho question of whether tho church here is under the Ecclesiastical control and supervision of the Bishop of Antigua, I would observe, before closing tins communication, that 1 have long since been under the impression that there iB a letter extant from the Danish Government to the British Government, making the request that it should be so, a copy of which is said to

be in the Archives of the Secretary's Office here. But, be this as it may, there is one thing certain, that if it is not so, the proper course might to be adopted at once to put this and otl >r questions, touching the interest of the church, beyond doubt one way or another, in order not to be liable to have rendered nugatory the legitimate authority which the clergyman lias a right to exercise in the church for the suppression of vice and immorality, by n strained right of interference founded upon an antiquated law inapplicable to the case, subversive of the free exercise of wholesome religious restraint, and repugnant to the spirit and Intelligence of the times we live in. B. C. A.

Mr þÿEditor, The correspondence which has lately taken place between certain members of St. John's Church and the Vestry on the subject of the views adopted by the present Rector and his representative, with regard to the Baptism of Infants &e., in direct opposition to the Canons of t lie Episcopal Church, being now before the public, I venture to call attention to the dissatisfaction at present unhappily existing in the many of the members of that church ou this sulj ct, and to offer for their consideration the only remedy, which, from the position assumed by the Vestry, appears now left for their adoption. In doing this I would not merely allude tn the subject of Baptism, but more especially to the general tendency evinced by all tho Rector's discourses, delivered in the church and elsewhere, since assuming his p sit ion, to produce one of tbeso fearful out- " Revival," religious breaks of than which, to tny mind, no more fanaticism, known as a baneful oi detrimental influence could arise, for the injury of our already depressed community, excifing thereby the minds of the ignorant and superstitious io the most exaggerated impulses. In support of tny views on this subject, I would refer tn what is now going on in the unfortunate Island of Jamaica (which Island appeai s for years to have been the battle ground of religions differences) as reported in the newspapers of 8 li Feb uuy und 9th April and London l imes 16 It and 18' h March, as also to the well known effects of " Revivalism"

witnessed among the smaller English Islands under the guidance of the Wesleyan body. The proof is bclore our eyes, and we need travel no farther than our neigliboui hood for its development. As I understand the constitution of the Episcopal church in this Island, it is a voluntary establishment, supported wholly from funds contributed by its members, presided over by, and subject io, the dictum of no Bishop, appointing through the Vestry its own clergy, with the power to dispense with their services whenever found to be otherwise than conducive to the order, peace, and well being of the congregation, and guided in its government ( especially on account of its insulated position) by the Cations of the Episcopal church ot Euglaud, notwithstanding the words of 'he Right Reverend Bishop Davis (whose judgment, the by, by never stood paramount in his own Diocese) quoted by the Vestry, and consequently, having the sole control ol its finances, with an unfettered judgment as to their disbursement. The privilege of appeal to the Vestry by a member of (he congregation in case of grievance from any overt act of the Rector, conceded by the Vestry's letter, I consider undoubted. This privilege lias been exercised in the present instance, liow far to the satisfaction of the parlies concerned, I leave them fo say ; and I would ask, and 1 do so with pain, whether a large portion of the congregation, especially of that portion referred to by the Vestry as "unqualified by the measure

of their own intelligence or judgment to form a correct opinion" þÿ are to be excluded from their religious rights, the peace of the community or jeopardized, by the introduction of, to us at least, such moral doctrines as do not accord with the ru'es hitherto looked up to as the guide and safeguard of the church. The authority of the Canons and usages of the church appear to bo ignored in the letter of the officiating Minister, published by the Vestry but I would assert, and without fear of con- ; tradiction, that under the English Government, whether of Church or State, and as far as my knowledge "f tho Bible goes, none arc above the Law, be they Primate or Prime Minister, Priest or Layman.

What redress then does the Letter of the Vestry offer lor has appeal to them " failed, the kind advice not to permit evil counsel, our present difficulties ? The except in elicit ing or the vehemence of passiou to take capiive their better feelings and more deliberate judgment and it is in vain we L.ok to that of the officiating Minister for any happier omen þÿ there all appears settled and immutable Again 1 ask, from what quarter is redress to be sought ? To my mind the answer is plain, clear, and simple. Driven by the Vestry's decision and the Minister's resolve, let that portion of the congregation who do not desire to hear religious controversy and disunion preached seek redress from themselves, and cease to support a Ministry they cannot approve of. The power lies in their own hands. Aet firmly, and the existing Evils must soon be replaced by a return to those days of peace, prosperity, and contentment, enjoyed for 13 long years in the church of St John's, under the mild and wise Ministry of our late lameuted Rector, the Revd. Doctor llawley. St. Croix 22ud April 1861. Z

To the Editor of the St. Croix Avis. Dear Sir ! In perusing the letter of the officiating minister, Mr. Williams, addressed to the "Vestry of St. John's Church," I could not help remarking the unhappy quotation employed by the reverend gentlemen "to establish in the minds of the ignorant masses, this all-absorbing truth; ' that neither circumcision, nor uncircumcision, neither baptism nor confiiination, neither marriage nor the Lord's supper avails any thing,' but a new creature." Now, Sir, this I think is rather n death-blow to the innovation attempted by the reverend Mr. Williams: for if baptism and marriage avail nothing , why does lie deny the one to the children and urge the other on the parents? Is it not very plain if he himself n gard not baptism as availing anything, he undoubtedly believes that parents regard it as arm7iwg(ifnot every thing) something; since, from the tact of his refusing to baptize their children, he must hope to constrain them reason though it be for no other into getting married, than that their children might be legitimate, and so be fit candidates for baptism. Again. The reverend gentleman remarks that " no protectant dissenter baptizes illegitimate children while the parents are unmarried or have not professed repentance þÿ no Independent, þÿ no Moravian, þÿ no Presbyterian, þÿ no Wesljan.'' Why, I would ask, influence example senters or Moravians should the his conduct to of dissuch a degree as to cause htm to deviate from the prescribed rules of his own church, and so violate his oidination vow? It is certain he

vowed to hold inviolate the Canons of the Church to which he was ordained ; yet we find him violating, directly, ' to christen," on the ground, as it appears, Canon 68, try refusing that Independents, Moravians, Presbyterians, and Wesleyans, do so. From this I am rather inclined to infer that Mr. Williams and his constituent. Mr. Almon, stand rather alone in this matter, so far as the church in which they minister is concerned ; though he, Mr. W. says that, "not only has the Bishop Kingston of recommended and commended the adoption of the course he is now pursuing in St John's Church with regard to illegitimate children, and which he has pursued for some years in Jamaica : but there are very few of the clergy in that island who do not find it necessary to act on this plan, in order to put a stop to the on-going immorality amongst the .peasantry, as well as, he from amongst others who should, is sorry to add, their position in Society, be barriers to, rather than promotersof profligacy and notorious concubinage." But let me ask. Will tho Bishop of King-ton stand up for Mr. Williams and suppor t trim against tho Canons of the Church of England of which he is one of the bishop- 1 Or will the "highly commendatory opinion of the present Bishop of Antigua, pronounced on Iris theological views and sentiment" help him out ol the scrape into which he has got. himself? I rather think notþÿ though with all dne deference to his lordship's opinion þÿ therefore it would be best, if the "views" are like the "ro«r»e" he is now

Ss T. in. 0 I. « \f I) pursuing, that he would reserve those views and that course for some more lueky sphere. Before leaving this painfully interesting subject altogether 1 must advance this opinion: that, though differences may frequently arise, they would not continue so long in the church, if a light, unbia-et, unprejudiced view were always taken of all matters connected with it: and such measures adopted by tho-e in whose hands the affairs of the church are intrusted, as would show to the parties concerned, that a strict adherence to the rules, influences them; and not forward such quibbles as the being "actuated by the best aud purest motives," and therefore, þÿ "however opinions may differ as to the mode adopted þÿ ought at least to he allowed the merit of good intentions," in extenuation of any wrong course whatever, adopted by the clergyman or otheis: or that a Vestry has "no authotity to direct or govern a clergyman's conduct in Ecclesiastical matters," though they he the most presumptuous violation of the Canons of the Church, as the case in question is of Canon 68, as well as tlie27fh of the Thirty-nine Articles, louud in the Book of Common Prayer. Iu both the parishes the peace of the church has, more than once, been interrupted by dissensions and difference, brought about by some new-fangled dogma; some party-spiiit; soine attempt at drawing the uncharitable line of demai cation, between this people and that people ; or the greater evil of the minority (taking the advantage of their position) attempting to

Russia & Poland The lessons read to the Austrian and Italian Sovereigns by the events of the last two years have not been lost on the Emperor ol Russia, lie has dealt like a sensible man with the disturbance at Warsaw. Ten year ago the city would have swum with blood. Sucli a demonstration as that on the anniversary of the battle of Grochow would have roused the late Czar to fury. Troops would have been at once moved on Warsaw', the streets would have been cleared by artillery, the leaders, real or suspected, of the movement would have been shot or transported to Siberia, hundreds of young men would have been draughted into the army, estates would have been confiscated, contributions levied, and, finally, alter a tierce and unnecessary repression, þÿ order would have resigned at þÿWarsaw. Monarehs, however, arc now likely to be wiser or more merciful. They will recognize either that to promote their subþÿjects happiness is a moral duty, or that it. is an able policy. The history of Europe during thirty years has thought them that in the long run every nation revenges itself on unpopular rulers. Either it throws off the yoke, or it compels the maintenance of such an army as brings bankruptcy on the oppressing State, or it weakens the Sovereign in presence of his rivals.

They seem to have had nothing in common with the Western Democracy, which is the mure singular, since in 1830 the late of Charles X was certainly the cause of the outbreak which followed at Warsaw. An answer has been received Irotn St. Petersburg, graciously conceding almost all that was demanded.
